row.basis: lost traveler, missing road and city
row.note: The commentary's traveler cannot find either the route or its home; the psalm's wilderness wanderers likewise find no way to an inhabited city.

row.basis: led by a straight way to a city
row.note: The psalm answers the same route-and-destination crisis by saying that God led the wanderers by a straight way until they reached a city to live in.

row.basis: God led a servant to a household
row.note: The commentary says guidance shows both road and house; Abraham's servant credits God with leading him on the way to his master's brothers' house.

row.basis: a messenger goes before, guards, brings to a place
row.note: The angel is sent ahead to guard Israel on the way and bring them to a prepared place, closely joining the forward guide, the route, and its destination.

row.basis: God goes ahead and shows the way
row.note: The wilderness guide goes before the people, seeks their camping place, and shows the way they are to go, matching the commentary's threefold guide image.

row.basis: pillar before the people, light for travel
row.note: The cloud and fire travel ahead to lead Israel by the way and give light for movement, combining a visible sign with a guide who precedes.

row.basis: ark goes before to seek a resting place
row.note: The ark moves before the camp in order to seek a resting place, a communal version of a guide already ahead on the road toward a home.

row.basis: voice says this is the way when one turns
row.note: The voice behind the traveler identifies the way precisely when rightward or leftward deviation threatens, giving a direct counterpart to remaining on the straight line.

row.basis: blind led on unknown paths and rough ground levelled
row.note: The passage has God lead those who do not know the route, turn darkness to light, and make rough places level, gathering guidance, signs, and road surface in one scene.

row.basis: straight path without stumbling on return
row.note: The returning community is led by waters on a straight path where it will not stumble; this adds a homeward communal return to the requested unerring path.

row.basis: teacher leads in the way to go
row.note: God both teaches what benefits and leads the people in the way they should go, supplying the instructional dimension of ihdinā without reducing it to information alone.

row.basis: God makes paths straight
row.note: The proverb makes straight paths the result of acknowledging God in all one's ways, an ethical counterpart to asking to be led onto a straight route.

row.basis: holy highway where walkers do not go astray
row.note: The prophetic highway is explicitly a way on which even the unwise do not err, directly meeting the commentary's contrast between the straight path and those who lose it.

row.basis: prepare and make a highway straight
row.note: The call to prepare a way and make a desert highway straight supplies a constructed-road image for the commentary's straight, made passable path.

row.basis: levelled valleys, mountains, crooked and rough ground
row.note: The text makes a road by levelling terrain and straightening crookedness; it sharpens the commentary's physical account of a path becoming smooth under passage.

row.basis: build up the road and remove its obstacle
row.note: The command to prepare the way by removing an obstruction from the people's route makes explicit the work needed for an unobstructed communal path.

row.basis: road markers and guideposts for return
row.note: The prophet tells returning Israel to set up markers and guideposts and attend to the highway, the closest terrestrial sign-and-wayfinding scene beside the commentary.

row.basis: build highway, clear stones, raise a signal
row.note: The city-bound road is built up, cleared of stones, and marked by a raised signal, combining surface preparation and public landmarks.

row.basis: mountains made into a way
row.note: The passage turns mountains themselves into a road and raises highways for return, connecting the commentary's mountain landmark with a navigable, homeward route.

row.basis: king's highway with no right or left turn
row.note: The travelers pledge to keep the king's highway and not turn to either side, a literal-road analogue to the commentary's insistence on staying in the road's middle.

row.basis: foot holds the prior step and does not turn aside
row.note: Job describes his foot as holding fast to God's step, keeping God's way, and not turning aside; it makes following a preceding trace an act of fidelity.

row.basis: a teacher leads in paths of uprightness
row.note: The sage says he has taught the way of wisdom and led the pupil in upright paths, giving the human teacher-guide form of the commentary's leading guide.

row.basis: level the track of the feet
row.note: The pupil is told to make level the track of the feet so that all ways are firm, closely matching the commentary's attention to feet and a route's walkable surface.

row.basis: do not turn right or left
row.note: The command against lateral departure supplies the moral form of the commentary's straight line and its threatening directions on either side.

row.basis: ask for ancient paths and walk the good way
row.note: The people are told to seek out the ancient paths, identify the good way, and walk it; this gives the route an inherited communal history rather than treating it as private discovery.

row.basis: many peoples taught God's ways and walking his paths
row.note: Nations gather to receive instruction and then say they will walk in God's paths, directly pairing a guide's teaching with a community's shared road.

row.basis: Heb. עבד and Ar. نعبد; walking all God's ways
row.note: Deuteronomy joins walking in all God's ways with serving God, and its Hebrew עבד is cognate with the commentary's Arabic نعبد; its own context keeps service covenantal while pairing it with a walked way.

row.basis: walk after God, obey, serve, cling
row.note: The verse orders Israel to walk after God and then to obey, serve, and cling to him, making worship a following relation rather than a detached rite.

row.basis: a people walks in its god's name
row.note: Each people is said to walk in its god's name, while the speaker's community walks in the LORD's name forever; this gives the road the collective identity developed in Fātiḥa 1:7.

row.basis: Heb. קוממיות and Ar. مستقيم; walking upright
row.note: God frees Israel from slavery and makes them walk upright; Hebrew קוממיות and the commentary's q-w-m form in مستقيم share the root while the verse ties upright walking to release from servitude.

row.basis: Heb. נעם and Ar. أنعمت; pleasant ways
row.note: The personified Wisdom has ways of pleasantness and paths of peace; Hebrew נעם is cognate with the n-ʿ-m family named for أنعمت, though the biblical verse speaks of Wisdom's pleasant path rather than a gloss on bestowed favor.

row.basis: blessed people whose way is blameless
row.note: The psalm calls blessed those blameless in way who walk in the LORD's instruction, a concise counterpart to the favored community's path.

row.basis: lamp for feet and light for path
row.note: Word as a lamp for feet and a light for a path turns guidance into a visible orientation aid, alongside the commentary's signs that let a traveler find the way.

row.basis: sheep stray, each turns to its own way
row.note: The all-sheep image and the phrase each to its own way make dispersion the opposite of a single communal route, matching the commentary's scattered groups and lost travelers.

row.basis: shepherds lead sheep astray from their resting place
row.note: The people's shepherds make them wander from mountain to hill until they forget their resting place, a concentrated inverse of a leading guide who brings a traveler home.

row.basis: scattered sheep without a shepherd
row.note: The sheep scatter because there is no shepherd and become prey, furnishing the social danger behind the commentary's image of people dispersing in every direction.

row.basis: sheep wander on mountains and none searches
row.note: The sheep wander over mountains and hills and across the earth with no searcher, a landscape-scale portrait of the daḷḷīn as lost travelers.

row.basis: crooked paths and no known way of peace
row.note: The wicked neither know the way of peace nor walk a straight course, because their paths are made crooked; it gives a moral inverse to both straightness and guided arrival.

row.basis: a way seems right but ends in death
row.note: The proverb warns that apparent rightness can conceal a road whose end is death, qualifying the commentary's contrast of the straight course with a destructive destination.

row.basis: path of life rising away from Sheol
row.note: The wise person's path of life turns upward from Sheol, a sharp counterpart to the commentary's deliberately inverted guidance to the road of Gehenna.

row.basis: blessed person does not walk in the wicked's counsel
row.note: The opening beatitude defines a favored walker by refusing the wicked's counsel and way, giving the two paths distinct human company.

row.basis: judgment and assembly of righteous
row.note: The wicked cannot stand in judgment or in the assembly of the righteous, joining Fātiḥa's reckoning day to its differentiated communal destinies.

row.basis: the LORD knows the righteous way, wicked way perishes
row.note: The final contrast names a way known by God and a way that perishes, providing both divine oversight and a terminal division of routes.

row.basis: ancient roads abandoned for bypaths
row.note: The people forget God, stumble from ancient roads, and take a bypath rather than a highway; this is a particularly close inverse of the well-worn main track.

row.basis: a walker cannot direct his own steps
row.note: Jeremiah denies that a person walking can direct his own steps, making a request for divine guidance necessary rather than merely desirable.

row.basis: messenger prepares a way before the Lord
row.note: The messenger who prepares the way before the Lord is a forerunner figure, relevant to the commentary's definition of a guide as one who moves ahead.

row.basis: Wisdom guides on straight paths and shows a kingdom
row.note: Wisdom guides the fleeing righteous person on straight paths and shows him God's kingdom, unusually preserving together the straight route, guide, and disclosed destination.

row.basis: ask God to direct paths
row.note: Tobit's parental instruction tells the traveler to ask God to direct his paths and make his plans prosper, a prayer-shaped analogue to ihdinā.

row.basis: a companion knows the road to Media
row.note: The prospective companion answers that he knows the road and has traveled it often, a concrete narrative instance of the knowledgeable guide required for a journey.

row.basis: mountains lowered so Israel walks safely
row.note: God levels mountains and fills valleys so Israel may walk safely in glory, closely echoing the commentary's made-passable straight road and communal return.

row.basis: sinners' smooth paved way ending in Hades
row.note: Sirach calls the sinners' way smoothly paved yet says it ends in Hades; it complicates the beaten or easy road image with the commentary's opposing road to Gehenna.

row.basis: straying from truth's way
row.note: The impious confess that they strayed from the way of truth and did not know the Lord's way, directly joining lost direction with a missed moral destination.

row.basis: which straight way should a person choose
row.note: The mishnah asks which derekh yesharah a person should choose and answers ethically, an explicit rabbinic reading of straightness as a practiced, publicly accountable way of life.

row.basis: two spirits in which humans walk
row.note: The Community Rule says humans have spirits of truth and perversity in which to walk, framing communal moral travel as a divided field rather than an undifferentiated road.

row.basis: Jesus says he is the way to the Father
row.note: The commentary cites Jesus calling worship of God the straight path; John instead has Jesus identify himself as the way by which one comes to the Father, so the differing identification of the path is the point.

row.basis: shepherd goes ahead and sheep follow
row.note: The shepherd brings out his own sheep, goes before them, and they follow his voice, closely matching the commentary's guide who walks in front and a community that follows.

row.basis: star goes before travelers to a house
row.note: The star moves before the travelers until it stands over the child's location, an unusually exact Christian convergence of star-sign, forward guide, and destination.

row.basis: light guides feet into the way of peace
row.note: The dawn/light is said to guide feet into the way of peace, turning the commentary's orientation signs into an explicitly footed, divinely directed route.

row.basis: messenger sent before to prepare the way
row.note: Mark applies the forerunner formula to John, whose going before prepares the Lord's way; this is a Christian scriptural development of the guide-ahead image.

row.basis: make the Lord's paths straight
row.note: Mark's wilderness proclamation uses straightened paths as preparation for the Lord's arrival, interpreting prophetic road building as an advent scene.

row.basis: broad road with many leads to destruction
row.note: The broad road's many travelers and destructive end give a concrete Christian counterpart to the commentary's dispersed alternatives to the one path.

row.basis: narrow way found by few leads to life
row.note: The way that leads to life is constrained and found by few, placing a decisive destination and a defined route beside the requested straight path.

row.basis: crooking the Lord's straight ways
row.note: The opponent is accused of making the Lord's straight ways crooked, an exact verbal and moral inverse to keeping a course mustaqīm.

row.basis: not walking straight toward gospel truth
row.note: Paul says certain conduct is not walking straight toward the gospel's truth, making upright walking a communal ethical test rather than a mere route description.

row.basis: make straight paths for feet
row.note: The congregation must make straight paths for its feet so that the lame are healed rather than put out of joint, adding care for vulnerable walkers to the road image.

row.basis: forsaking the straight way and going astray
row.note: The false teachers explicitly abandon the straight way and wander into Balaam's course, one of the closest New Testament inversions of the commentary's daḷḷīn.

row.basis: straying sheep returned to shepherd and overseer
row.note: The audience was straying like sheep but has returned to the shepherd and overseer of souls, combining lostness, return, and a restoring guide.

row.basis: walker in darkness does not know where going
row.note: The person who walks in darkness cannot know the destination because darkness blinds the eyes, a direct cognitive and spatial rendering of being lost.

row.basis: walk as the exemplar walked
row.note: The one who remains in Christ is obliged to walk as he walked, making a prior walk an exemplary track for later followers.

row.basis: love is walking according to commandments
row.note: The epistle defines love as walking according to God's commandments, directly coupling the commentary's worshipful path with repeated ethical practice.

row.basis: wanderer from truth brought back
row.note: The community is charged with bringing back anyone who wanders from truth, closely paralleling the commentary's companions calling the bewildered person back to guidance.

row.basis: blind guide and blind follower fall into a pit
row.note: The saying makes the guide's competence decisive: a blind guide leads another blind person into a pit, the perilous inverse of a guide who knows the road.

row.basis: worship according to the Way
row.note: Paul says that he worships the ancestral God according to the Way, showing a Christian community in which worship and a named collective road are one identity.

row.basis: walk in Abraham's footsteps
row.note: The faithful are described as walking in Abraham's footsteps, a precise ancestral-track analogue to the commentary's path already passed over by others.

row.basis: the Lamb shepherds and guides to life-water
row.note: The Lamb shepherds the multitude and guides it to springs of life-water, retaining the forward guide and a life-giving destination at the end of collective trial.

row.basis: following the Lamb wherever he goes
row.note: The faithful follow the Lamb wherever he goes, giving the commentary's community-behind-a-leader image an eschatological Christian form.

row.basis: new and living way through the veil
row.note: The passage calls access through the sanctuary veil a new and living way, making the route itself the means of reaching God's dwelling presence.

row.basis: the way of life and the way of death
row.note: The Didache's opening two-ways instruction turns path language into a catechetical division between life and death, a compact Christian interpretive frame for the single way and its opposed courses.

row.basis: Heb. מלך and Ar. مَٰلِكِ; king's highway
row.note: Hebrew מלך and the m-l-k form named in the commentary are cognate, while the verse's king's highway is a literal road; it supports the road association without making its royal noun a definition of Fātiḥa's owner.

row.basis: Heb. דין and Ar. ٱلدِّين
row.note: Rachel says that God has judged her with a d-y-n form cognate with Arabic dīn; it illuminates the commentary's reckoning sense, though this narrative has no path image and does not establish the secondary habit sense.

row.basis: din and reckoning before the King of kings
row.note: Avot's formula of giving din and reckoning before the King of kings gives a Jewish eschatological account-setting beside Fātiḥa's owner of the day of dīn, rather than its road-wordplay.

row.basis: walking after God as imitating divine deeds
row.note: The talmud asks how a human can walk after God in Deuteronomy and answers by imitating God's acts of care; this interpretation turns following the divine way into daily embodied service.

row.basis: Father's house and a prepared place
row.note: The many dwelling places and prepared place in the Father's house make explicit the destination side of the commentary's claim that guidance shows a road together with its house.

row.basis: Isaiah's terrain-leveling in a John the Baptist setting
row.note: Luke retains the levelling of valleys, mountains, crookedness, and roughness as preparation for salvation, giving the road construction image a distinct Christian forerunner setting.

row.basis: observe those who walk by an apostolic example
row.note: The community is asked to imitate and watch people whose walk conforms to an established example, an explicit social pattern for the commentary's already-walked road.

row.basis: God directs a journey's way
row.note: Paul asks God and the Lord Jesus to direct his way to the recipients, a specific travel prayer that supplies a less developed but concrete guide-to-destination parallel.

row.basis: hearts go astray and do not know God's ways
row.note: The citation describes a people always going astray in heart and not knowing God's ways, joining inner deviation to the lost-way language without the commentary's literal traveler scene.

row.basis: wandering stars reserved for darkness
row.note: Jude calls the false teachers wandering stars destined for darkness; as an inverse to the commentary's stars used for orientation, the link is specific but the text does not portray them as travel guides.

row.basis: shepherd leads in paths of righteousness
row.note: The shepherd restores the traveler and leads him in righteous tracks, a direct shepherd-guide form of the requested path.

row.basis: rod and staff in the dark valley
row.note: The commentary's staff goes ahead as a guide; in this walking-through-danger scene the shepherd's rod and staff comfort the traveler, giving the object a related but not identical role.

row.basis: dwelling in the LORD's house
row.note: The psalm's guided traveler ends by dwelling in the LORD's house, supplying the homeward terminus paired with the commentary's route.

row.basis: righteousness goes before and makes a way
row.note: Righteousness goes before God and makes a way from his steps, a poetic image of a preceding presence whose passage establishes the route.

row.basis: good Spirit leads on level ground
row.note: The prayer asks for the good Spirit to lead the speaker on level ground, directly combining divine guidance with the commentary's flat, passable road.

row.basis: snares laid beside a path
row.note: The enemies spread nets and snares beside the path, a close physical counterpart to the hostile figure waiting upon and around the straight way.

row.basis: make me walk in the path of commandments
row.note: The psalmist asks to be made to walk in the path of commandments because he delights in it, preserving both a prayer for guidance and ongoing habitual movement.

row.basis: teach the way to walk and the deed to do
row.note: Moses is to make known the way people must walk and the work they must do, joining instruction, route, and daily practice as the commentary does.

row.basis: show us the way to walk and what to do
row.note: The remnant asks God to show the particular way it should walk and the act it should perform, a communal prayer that closely parallels ihdinā.

row.basis: shepherd seeks scattered sheep on a dark day
row.note: God promises to seek his flock amid its scattering, extending the earlier lost-sheep scene into the restoring action of a true guide.

row.basis: seek the lost and bring back the strayed
row.note: The divine shepherd seeks the lost and brings back the strayed, directly answering the commentary's lost traveler and the companions who call him toward guidance.

row.basis: the LORD before and Israel's God behind
row.note: The return is protected by a God who goes before and also guards from behind, an illuminating reversal of the commentary's vulnerable traveler surrounded by threats.

row.basis: priest walks in peace and uprightness, turns many
row.note: The exemplary priest walks with God in peace and uprightness and turns many from iniquity, joining straight conduct with a guide's effect on others.

row.basis: teachers cause many to stumble by instruction
row.note: The corrupt priests cause many to stumble through their teaching, a precise institutional inverse to the knowledgeable guide who keeps followers from losing the way.

row.basis: highway joining nations in shared worship
row.note: A highway enables movement between Egypt and Assyria and culminates in shared worship; it gives the commentary's communal worship-road an international, reconciliatory form.

row.basis: Wisdom guides by way, shelter by day, stars by night
row.note: Wisdom guides the holy people along a remarkable way and becomes their shelter by day and starlight by night, unusually gathering guide, road, and celestial orientation signs.

row.basis: walking God's way and lasting peace
row.note: Baruch says that walking God's way would have meant living in peace forever, a concise route-to-destination formulation.

row.basis: God leads Israel with joy in light
row.note: Following its road-leveling scene, Baruch says God will lead Israel with joy in the light of divine glory, adding visible guidance to the returning community.

row.basis: narrow city-road bordered by fire and water
row.note: The angel's image of the one narrow entrance to a city, with fire on one side and deep water on the other, makes remaining on a central course a matter of reaching one's home.

row.basis: traveler consults the Creator before setting out
row.note: The talmud identifies consulting God before a journey with the traveler's prayer, giving a rabbinic liturgical practice for seeking protection and direction on a road.

row.basis: following the light avoids darkness
row.note: Jesus says that the one following him will not walk in darkness but will have the light of life, directly linking leader, walking, light, and non-lost arrival.

row.basis: walker in darkness does not know the destination
row.note: The warning to walk while light is present says darkness overtakes the person who walks without knowing where he goes, a close counterpart to the commentary's disoriented traveler.

row.basis: serving Jesus, following him, being where he is
row.note: The commentary's cited Jesus directs worship to God as the straight path; John joins serving Jesus to following him and being where he is, so the object of service and path-following differs materially.

row.basis: Spirit of truth guides into all truth
row.note: The Spirit is promised as a guide into all truth; the guidance is interpretive rather than a road scene, but it preserves the commentary's leading rather than mere information.

row.basis: angel directs Philip onto the Gaza road
row.note: An angel sends Philip onto a specific desert road, making divine guidance an actual route instruction before the encounter with the traveler.

row.basis: unless someone guides me
row.note: On the road, the Ethiopian says he cannot understand unless someone guides him, a direct verbal and scene-level counterpart to needing a guide for the way.

row.basis: instructed in the way of the Lord
row.note: Apollos is instructed in the way of the Lord and teaches concerning Jesus, giving the Way an explicit pedagogical form alongside the commentary's guide who makes a path known.

row.basis: blind man gains sight and follows on the way
row.note: The healed blind man immediately follows Jesus on the way, bringing sight, recovery from disorientation, and following a leader into one movement.

row.basis: self-styled guide of the blind and light in darkness
row.note: Paul reports the claim to be a guide of blind people and a light in darkness in a critical context; it provides a qualified counterexample to the authority of a guide.

row.basis: those led by God's Spirit are God's children
row.note: The verse makes being led by God's Spirit a defining relation of God's children, an abstract but specific counterpart to a community guided by God.

row.basis: good works prepared beforehand to walk in
row.note: God prepares good works beforehand so that believers may walk in them, making a divinely prepared course the form of sustained practice.

row.basis: walk worthy toward God's kingdom and glory
row.note: Paul urges conduct worthy of the God who calls believers into kingdom and glory, joining a moral walk to a destination beyond the journey.

row.basis: way into the sanctuary not yet manifest
row.note: The Spirit indicates that the way into the holy place was not yet open, supplying the inaccessible-side context for the later new and living way.

row.basis: heavenly homeland and a prepared city
row.note: The pilgrims seek a better, heavenly homeland and God prepares a city for them, a destination image that complements the commentary's road-and-house pairing.

row.basis: no lasting city here, seeking the coming one
row.note: The community has no permanent city here and seeks the coming city, turning road imagery into an ongoing search for a final dwelling.

row.basis: nations walk by the city's light
row.note: The nations walk by the New Jerusalem's light, an eschatological convergence of collective travel, orienting light, and the city as destination.
